speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
that Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us today amends the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. It seeks to raise substantial new revenues from the commodity tax system. While no Government likes to raise taxes, this Bill clearly reflects the Government's determination to achieve the economic renewal goals of the May 1985 Budget. These measures emphasize the Government's continued commitment to fairness in its approach to policies, programs and people as outlined in the May Budget. These measures, for instance, reflect a number of objectives in the Budget which address the need for greater fairness in our tax system.
Before I address the substance of the Bill, I want to point out to Hon. Members that the principles of this Government's Budget can be seen as the right prescription for the times. For example, witness recent economic indicators, as well as forecasts published by both the Economic Council of Canada and the Royal Bank of Canada.
Since September, 1984-in one year-we have seen the Government's policies restore economic confidence in the country. This Government's policies will see that Canada does indeed become a land of prosperity. We are beginning to see what the dismantling of the National Energy Program can do to our energy sector. Already, exploration activity is beginning to increase and the prospects of long-term domestic supply of energy reserves are improving. Also, the Government's shift in job training strategy from makeshift and make-work projects toward long-term career-oriented skills training will bolster our economy by employing productively more and more Canadians.
This Government's forward-looking policies have already created 305,000 jobs. We look to the expansion of the economy to further reduce unemployment. Today's unemployment level
of 10.1 per cent is the lowest it has been in three years-not low enough for this Government. We shall continue to promote policies which create meaningful work for Canadians.
We have seen about 155,000 new housing starts this past year as well. This bodes well for the construction industry. In the past year, interest rates on mortgages have continued to drop. We have seen the interest rate on one-year mortgages fall 2.75 percentage points to 10 per cent; and we have seen the reintroduction of the five-year mortgage. This is, indeed, good news, not just to those engaged in the construction sector but to Canadians everywhere who want to own their own home.
Early this week the Royal Bank of Canada confirmed that economic growth in this country is proceeding at a steady pace, that inflation and interest rates will continue to decline and unemployment will be at its lowest level in years. The Royal Bank says that the Canadian economy is looking better because Canadian businesses are spending more money, producting more goods and employing more people.
Along with certain tax increases in our May Budget, this Budget also introduced a capital gains tax exemption. It is this capital gains tax exemption which is encouraging investment by small and medium-sized business. It is this Government's initiative which is helping to restore optimism, confidence and prosperity in this great country of ours.
I would now like to turn to some of the tax measures we introduced in the May Budget in order to bring the deficit under control and to manage Government more effectively to achieve and sustain the benefits of economic growth which we are just beginning to enjoy. Our policies, to wrestle the deficit and manage the Government better, are part of a comprehensive set of actions designed to deal with a wide range of economic and fiscal needs.
We must manage to control the deficit and administer Government operations more efficiently, if we are to reap the benefits of economic renewal and consolidate those benefits.
We must achieve these goals through a series of comprehensive measures aimed at responding to a broad range of economic and financial needs.

The Bill should, therefore, be viewed in the context of all of the changes and proposals which were announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in May. As a fiscal initiative, this Bill concentrates heavily on the control of the national debt through a number of revenue-raising measures and reductions in tax expenditures. To achieve more effective

October 24, 1985
Excise Tax Act
Government management, this Bill implements many of the recommendations of the ministerial task force on program review.
To improve tax fairness, the Bill introduces a comprehensive system of assessments, objections and appeals. It provides protection for taxpayers from collection action with respect to amounts in dispute until the issue has been settled by the courts. The decision to increase taxes was taken after much soul-searching and in light of the very serious economic situation in which we find ourselves as a nation.
The national debt, as we have said many times, is unacceptably large and growing at a dramatic rate. The magnitude of the deficit and debt problem poses serious risks to our ability to achieve economic renewal and sustained economic growth. It is only by tough measures to take control of the deficit that the Government of Canada can avoid a financial and economic morass. Uncontrolled increases in the deficit and the debt would not only frustrate efforts to foster further economic growth but would also jeopardize many existing Government programs which provide services to the public.
Inaction, in light of these facts, would be an abdication of responsibility. The hard decisions and dramatic changes reflected in this Bill show that this Government can and will face its responsibilities.
The deficit affects us all and it threatens us all. Deficit control measures must be shared as broadly as possible if results of the magnitude required are to be achieved. Therefore, effective January 1, 1986, all the ad valorem federal sales tax rates will increase by one percentage point. The federal sales tax applies to a broad range of goods purchased by all Canadians and while the impact of this change on individual purchases will be small, the increase will raise federal revenues in 1986 by an estimated $825 million.
This Bill also implements a two cents per litre excise tax which has applied since September 3, 1985, on gasoline, diesel fuel and aviation fuel. This two cent levy will generate $160 million in 1985 and some $930 million in the full year 1986.
In response to the May Budget proposals, Canadians showed that they strongly support deficit reduction and are willing to share in that effort. They are not only willing to participate but have shown their compassion in preferring broad measures to measures which raise anxieties and uncertainties within a financially vulnerable group. Thus, in response to public concern, this Bill contains the provision whereby the broad-based excise tax on gasoline, diesel fuel and aviation fuels will be increased by one cent per litre effective January 1, 1987, to help meet the continuing cost of fully indexing old age pensions. This measure will yield $450 million annually.
This Bill, Mr. Speaker, also rationalizes certain elements of the tax system. Prior to the May Budget, for example, the specific per unit excise levies on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products had been adjusted automatically in line with increases in the Consumer Price Index. This Government believes that increases in such excise levies in accordance with
a rigid formula are not appropriate. Therefore, the automatic indexation of these levies is being eliminated. Indexation of these levies would have resulted in a 4 per cent increase effective September 1, 1985. In its place, the levies on spirits, beer, and wine are being increased by 2 per cent effective from the budget date.
[ Translation]
The slight increase is in response to problems currently being experienced by certain parts of the alcoholic beverage industry. Subsequent increases will be submitted to Parliament from time to time, for consideration.
This Bill also makes it possible to improve the tax base by increasing excise levies on tobacco products. The increase works out to the equivalent of 1 per cent per cigarette, effective from the Budget date. The serious threat to health and the high cost to society of dealing with smoking-related illnesses are reflected in the substantial increases being proposed.

The over-all impact of the measures affecting alcoholic beverages and tobacco products will be to increase federal revenues by $135 million in 1985 and by $245 million in 1986. This Bill also implements a number of technical amendments. For instance, the Bill repeals the constraints on individuals who produce home-brewed beer for non-commercial use by themselves and their acquaintances. Home brewers of beer will now be treated similarly to persons who produce wine for personal consumption.
This Bill includes measures to improve Government effectiveness through better management in line with the first report of the ministerial task force on program review. In its report tabled with the Budget last May, the task force made a number of comments on the commodity tax system. In particular, the task force made the following observation:
The number of manufactured goods which have been exempted from federal sales tax or which have enjoyed reduced rates of tax has increased. This, in turn, has led to an erosion of the tax base and the need to impose higher tax rates on those remaining goods which are taxable. These exemptions have also created a complex network of boundary problems and inequities. Exemptions of individual goods have led to pressures to make similar goods, or goods of like class, also exempt from tax. Exemptions have also tended, in the absence of sunset provisions, to outlive the purpose for which they were initially granted.
Action is clearly needed to reverse this process of costly tax subsidies and expenditures that distort the normal functioning of the market-place. Even where benefits accrue to intended recipients, commodity tax exemptions have shown themselves to be very inefficient and costly. Often tax relief can be provided to a specific target group only by providing much broader and more general relief than is really desired. This increases the cost and extends relief to many persons who are in little need of Government assistance.
This Bill contains significant steps to counter the problems identified by the task force. Effective July 1, 1985 a range of goods for which exemption from federal sales tax has been provided will again be subject to tax. Goods affected by these measures include candy and confectionaries, soft drinks, pet
October 24, 1985

food, beauty and health goods and energy conservation material. Changes in the taxation of construction goods manufactured other than at the site of construction are also proposed. These goods will become taxable on their sale price rather than on the cost of materials as has been the case in the past.
Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker, that this is a tough Bill. It raises substantial new revenues by broadening the base of the federal sales tax and increasing the rates of tax. I am sure all Hon. Members recognize that the economic problems facing this country are not easy to solve, and in the Budget the need for economic growth, deficit reduction and job creation were addressed realistically. The measures announced in the Budget should be considered as a whole. The tax increases are balanced with Government expenditure reductions, and the impact of tax increases on the economy are balanced against tax decreases, the freeze on unemployment insurance premiums, the release of existing RHOSP funds into the economy, and major proposals to boost private initiative and productive investment throughout the economy. We faced the reality of deficit reduction and the fact that only strong and sustained policies such as these measures can restore the economic activity which creates satisfying employment for Canadians. This Government has openly asked a wide range of taxpayers to contribute in a fair way. Together, the expenditure cuts and tax changes are an important and fair way of restoring fiscal order to this country.
I said it was a tough Bill but I believe it is also fair. It asks all Canadians to share in the effort to restore the fiscal health of our country. This Bill is an important step in addressing the serious financial deficits we face. Therefore, I ask Hon. Members to give their full support to this Bill and ensure its speedy consideration in this Chamber.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister certainly toed the Party line this morning when she introduced this Bill for second reading. It is too bad that the Minister has to do the dirty work of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). We now have confirmation in this morning's newspapers of what we suspected, namely, that the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougal!) was against the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank. Apparently she was overruled by the Minister of Finance and, of course, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

I ask you, Mr. Speaker. If the Minister brings the same insights to the Bill before the House today, I wonder whether deep down, she might not be opposed to the Bill. It is clear that this Bill is poorly drafted and unfair and that it will probably have a disastrous and totally negative impact on the Canadian economy.
If the Minister continues to present the point of view of the Minister of Finance, she may end up acting as a scapegoat for the Government and the Minister.
Excise Tax Act

The Minister of State for Finance cannot always count on the revelations before a judicial inquiry to reveal to the Canadian public that she is in fact exercising sound, independent judgment.
[ Translation]
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the Minister does not support the avalanche of taxes to be levied under this Bill.

Why do I say that, Mr. Speaker? I say it because I am convinced that the Minister is aware that these taxes will have a severe-I repeat, severe-dampening effect on the Canadian economy. They will reduce consumer demand and, as we already know from the most recent reports of Statistics Canada, they will be inflationary.
May I remind the House of the dollar impact of these proposed measures? The numbers I am about to present are based upon an analysis made by the Department of Finance, a document which, you may recall, was leaked on or about the date of the Budget. These taxes are indirect but they will hit hard at Canadian consumers. Looking at the departmental analysis we see that in 1986-87, the total of these taxes will come to something like $2.67 billion. I arrive at that number by totalling the sales tax base broadening, the sales tax rate increase, the tobacco excise tax, the alcohol levy and the energy excise tax. I have deducted the alcohol and tobacco indexation, which is $100 million. I have not deducted the Canadian ownership charge, which will come to approximately $921 million next year, nor the oil export charge. They should not have been deducted as the Government has done in making its presentations because there is no evidence that these reductions will be passed on to consumers at the pump. Indeed, we know that the other sales tax increases can only be borne by consumers.
Again, as we look at the Department's figures, moving to the fiscal year 1990-1991, we see that the total impact will be $4.1 billion. That is only part of the multi-million dollar tax bill which the Minister of Finance handed to us last May.
I would remind the House that the Minister of Finance himself admitted the obvious dampening effect of taxes of this magnitude. During a television interview on March 1, I believe, when questioned about his future Budget, he said that taxes are not the way to go because they will have a dampening effect on the economy. He went on to point out that he thought there was sufficient room on the expenditure side to get at the famous deficit. Apart from this issue of dampening consumer demands and putting inflationary pressure on the economy, there are certain sectors and industries that are especially hard hit by the taxes which the Minister described to us today as being fair.
The Government had almost nine months to prepare that Budget and evaluate the impact that these taxes would have on

October 24, 1985
Excise Tax Act
various sectors of the economy. Canadians, and certainly members of my caucus if not all Members of the House, cannot understand how the Government spent so much time preparing this Budget without accurately estimating the negative impact it would have on various sectors.
As the Minister knows, many groups made representations in preparation for the Budget. However, nearly all of them were stonewalled. Of course, our elderly finally broke down that stone wall last June when the Government finally backed down on deindexing the old age pension. Of course, as a countermeasure, the Government immediately increased the tax on fuel. However, the fact is that most groups have been stonewalled.
I have seen a copy of letters that have been sent from the office of the Minister of Finance. They are typical form letters, with a few modifications to let the individual groups know at least that the Government is aware of their name and address. However, they all contain the same rhetoric which we heard once more this morning from the Minister of State for Finance. It is the old rhetoric about the twin objective of economic renewal and deficit reduction. Of course, the letters inevitably contain one other comment that was also offered to us this morning by the Minister of State for Finance. They all contain words to the effect, "On balance, the Budget was designed to share the burden fairly among Canadians*. What a joke.
Of course, the fairness of the Budget is a main issue. I will only touch upon it very briefly because the question of fairness has been and will be spoken to at some length. The unfairness of the Budget is apparent on its face. Today I essentially want to talk about the impact of this Budget in a macro sense. However, I will simply refute the Minister's comments about fairness this morning by reminding her of the deindexing debate on old age pensions and the current deindexing debate on the-

-family allowances. She is probably aware of the representations made yesterday on Parliament Hill by people who are going to be affected in a very negative way by these recommendations and the impact of the measures contained in the Budget.
I remind her also that she is putting forward a massive sales tax increase. The Minister knows as well as anybody else that a tax increase on many of these items hits the low and middle-income people first and hits them the hardest. Sales taxes are, by definition, regressive. When the Minister comes in here and puts a tax on health care products, products essentially used for the most part by the elderly who have the lowest incomes, she knows she is hitting the elderly in their pocket books. She also knows from the report of the National Welfare Council that we have a lot of Canadians living below the poverty line and they are all consumers of these products. Yet she comes in here with a proposal to increase the tax on
these products and has the gall to stand up and say that this is fair. Admit that it is not fair and demonstrate to us that if it is not fair it is in some way justified, economically or otherwise. I suggest it is not only unfair but economically it is dumb.
Without spending much more time on the issue of fairness, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that history will record that this is probably the most unfair Budget ever. Of course, the Prime Minister himself has gone on the record with respect to the gaffe made in terms of the deindexation of old age pensions. I hope to see him on the record a number of times more before the year is out admitting to the gaffes that have been made in the other aspects of this Budget, which are equally unfair.
Enough on the issue of fairness. Is this Budget intelligent? Is this Budget a response to the economic requirements of Canada in 1985 as we look at the economic circumstances? I talked about the over-all dampening effect but I want to refer, as I said a moment ago, to certain specific sectors.
[ Translation]
The Minister is probably aware of the fact that hundreds of small- and medium-sized construction companies are going to lose their profit margins altogether, as a result of the 6 per cent tax on construction materials.
The customary fixed price contracts in this sector are going to be a major problem for many of our construction companies.
The Government totally ignored the very practical and, I must say, not very popular suggestion to introduce this tax gradually, allowing for these fixed price contracts and the usual problems in this sector. However, it seems the Minister was not conscious of the challenges and problems in the industry.

And the tax on fuel-
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we already know that according to the Tourism Industry Association of Canada, the 4 per cent increase in the price of gas is expected to cause 900,000 fewer U.S. tourists to come to Canada every year, while the resulting loss to our economy will be $135 million and probably 5,235 jobs. [English]
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the Minister in the pre-Budget analysis should have consulted-perhaps the industry was consulted-but should have taken that into account. This short-term measure with a view to deficit reduction has had probably a more than compensating negative impact in terms of lost revenues and lost jobs.
Let me look at the trucking sector for a moment in particular, again with respect to the tax on fuels. I want to demonstrate, Mr. Speaker, and I want to emphasize that this is one example that I have looked at and that 1 hope the Minister of State for Finance has looked at. Because the cost of commercial transportation fuel must be passed on to someone else, why did the Minister not measure the full impact of what that
October 24, 1985

would be? Who are those costs going to be passed on to? What is the impact on the competitive position of the Canadian trucking industry? What is the impact on Canadian consumers? Again it appears to me that no homework was done.
Anyone at all familiar with taxation knows that ultimately the buck has to stop somewhere, and when a tax is imposed on a corporation, when a tax is imposed on a trucker, that tax must be passed on in the cost of goods and services or, perhaps, in employees' incomes. It has to be passed on somewhere. Did the Minister of State for Finance or the Minister of Finance take the time to do an analysis of where this tax would actually end up? I suggest they could not have done it. Had they done so, they would never have come forward with this tax on our trucking sector.
The commercial transportation fuel has been exempt from the initial 1.5 cents per litre which was imposed several years ago. Now with this 2 cent increase as of September 1 plus, of course, all the provincial ad valorem taxes, we are likely to see a cost of approximately 3 cents a litre being imposed on the commercial fuel consumption in Canada. For inter-city truckers who carry something like three-quarters of all consumer goods and something like 80 per cent of all food products, this translates into almost 3 cents per mile. It does not end there because the transportation fuel will be hit once more at the end of the year with a 1 cent per litre increase plus the sales tax increase. The 1 cent a litre increase is to make up for the retreat from the deindexation proposal on old age pensions.
What are the pass through implications of a tax of this kind? I cite this as only one example, but it is one with which I am sure the Minister is familiar. First, the carrier who has to pay this tax has no choice. The carrier has to Find some way of passing through the entire cost. The carrier's capacity to do that is limited somewhat by the economic clout that that carrier has in the particular sector. Obviously some small carriers will probably not be able to pass on the tax as easily as large shippers.
To the extent that it is passed on, to the extent the carrier is able to go back to the shipper of those goods, of those tomatoes, of those products that go on to the shelves of our stores, les depanneurs, in the shopping markets, that is where it is going to add up, right in the pocket of the consumer. It makes it a regressive tax of the worst kind affecting, as I say in the case of inter-city trucking, something like 80 per cent of all goods that are shipped.
It is effectively a tax on distance, Mr. Speaker. It is a direct tax on distance. It is the same as a tax on alcohol or on cigarettes, yet we are applying it on distance. With all the regional difficulty we have in the transportation sector and the efforts we must make to ensure that those sectors benefit from comparable costs, imagine imposing a tax of 3 cents per mile on distance that can only be incorporated into the cost of goods that people in outlying regions must pay. It is outrageous and obviously not thought through.
What are the international implications? First, the Minister knows full well that U.S. truckers already enjoy a substantial advantage over their Canadian counterparts. At the present
Excise Tax Act
time they enjoy an advantage of something like 7 to 10 cents per fuel gallon vis-a-vis their Canadian competition.
[DOT] (U40)
The excise tax which is being imposed by the Minister in Bill C-80 will more than double the disadvantage Canadian truckers already suffer. That, coupled with the other cost factors which are being exacerbated by the policies of the Government, obviously puts Canada's international trucking business very much at risk vis-a-vis its U.S. competition. It is a signal to Canadian carriers that to survive in this market they will be better off with a U.S. base.
What does that mean? What does that imply? It implies lost economic opportunity, lost jobs and an increase in jobs and trucking activities south of the border. I am absolutely astonished if the Government intended to create that kind of competitive hardship for Canadian truckers. We see two things-a direct assault on the pocketbooks of consumers, as is the sales tax by including a fuel tax, and it places the Canadian trucking sector, which is already under siege, in a more disadvantaged position than before.
I hope the Minister is paying attention. I say to her that it is not too late to back down. It is not too late to apply a little economic common sense to the tax measures which have been brought before the House for discussion today.
Let me talk very briefly about another sector. The Minister intends to put a tax on health care products. Apart from the issue of fairness to which I referred earlier-the effect on the elderly and those least able to support the cost of health care products at the present time, never mind having an additional tax applied thereto-there is a much greater economic issue. The Government does not think long term. It is strictly interested in the statistical data for next year and perhaps prior to the next election. Has the Government addressed the issue of long-term increasing health costs? When we look at the statistics, we see that from a level of 5.6 per cent of GNP on health care in Canada in 1960, we have moved to 8.44 per cent in 1982, or $22 billion, and we see that trend continuing. I suggest that the way to get at this trend, to make health costs supportable and to reduce the amount of public sector expenditure on health costs in years ahead, is to have better preventive medicine. Fundamental to that is the ability of Canadians to purchase health care products at a reasonable cost. If anything, the cost should be reduced, not increased. It is an example of short-term thinking, placing long-term issues in serious jeopardy.
I suppose I share the belief of many in the House, many in my own riding and elsewhere, that indeed Canadians are prepared to make some sacrifices to get the deficit under control, to get the fiscal framework well defined and in order. However, when this Minister, who has been directly involved in expenditures which may amount to $2 billion to bail out Canadian banks, comes into the House and says, "Our concern is to get the deficit under control", pardon me if I regard that as somewhat of a joke.

October 24, 1985
Excise Tax Act
This Minister, her colleague in Finance and her other colleagues in Cabinet are squandering billions of dollars, and they come into the House and ask us to accept a tax on health care products. They ask us to accept taxes which will amount to something like $4 billion out of the hands of consumers by 1990-91. They ask us to accept taxes which will take over $2 billion out of the hands of consumers next year. She is effectively telling us that in 1986-87 consumers should pay for the bank bail-out; that is what she is telling us. There will be no deficit reduction under this Government. We have seen approximately $2 billion there. We have yet to know the full cost of the tax ruling in the Gulf acquisition. We started with number of $1 billion. Some have put it as high as $1.5 billion. An interview was given by one of the principals who said that it might be only half a billion. If we assume that the figure will be $1 billion, we are up to $3 billion.
Then the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) tells us that we will buy a half billion dollar ice-breaker. That is only the beginning. To come into the House and make a speech telling us that the taxes being imposed upon Canadian consumers are designed to get the finances of the country in order has to be one of the best jokes we have heard in this session. The way the Government is going, I am sure we will hear many more. It is pretty difficult for us to reconcile $3.5 billion of money squandered against tax increases which will have a medium and long-term serious impact upon the Canadian economy, a major impact upon consumers, and a major negative, unfair impact upon those consumers at the low end of the income scale.
We know the Budget is unfair. There will be much more said about that by my colleagues. We know that it is economically unsound. We also know from evidence in every jurisdiction that the best economic stimulus one can have, or the best bang for the buck as economists say, is a sales tax cut. Of course the corollary of that is that the worst thing that can be done for consumer demand in terms of dampening any possible strong economic recovery is a major sales tax increase. That is what we have in Bill C-80. It is economically unsound and unfair in every way.
I suggest that the Minister has good grounds to go back to her colleague, the Minister of Finance, and tell him what she really thinks. I hope the judgment which she apparently brought to bear initially in the Canadian Commercial Bank bail-out will prevail in this case. I hope she will exercise that same good judgment, foresight and sense of fairness to Canadian taxpayers. Had her initial decision been accepted, Canadian taxpayers would not have been called upon to fork out up to $2 billion. Just for the benefit of Hon. Members, I might say that there are something like 10 million to 11 million taxpayers in the country. When we are talking about $2 billion, we are talking about close to $200 on average out of the pockets of every taxpayer. I presume I am including all Members of the House and you, Mr. Speaker.
On behalf of the people of Canada, I say to the Minister that she should exercise that good judgment, go back to the Minister of Finance and tell him that the Bill which she has
been asked to sponsor on his behalf is wrong. It is wrong for Canada. It is unfair. It is not the remedy which we need today, in October, 1985.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to say a few words regarding Bill C-80. I remember so vividly in the period leading up to the September election of 1984 that the Conservatives continually talked about the need to simplify the tax system, that it was too complicated and too burdensome. As a matter of fact, the Income Tax Act is a massive document. Referring to the tax experts themselves, I will quote from one of the most recent publications on the news-stands wherein the author said: "A full understanding of the Income Tax Act is impossible. Even for the true tax expert it is impossible".
We have the Excise Tax Act and, when we returned to the House in the fall of 1985, the Government did not say that it was time to simplify that Act. It introduced Bill C-80, which is "only" 125 pages of changes to the Excise Tax Act. We should think about what we are doing for a moment. We are making the income tax system more complicated.

We are trying to make the excise tax and the income tax system more complicated, more exact and more precise. We are deleting a few things, adding a few things and adding a few more loopholes. Because of this, we are systematically biasing the tax system of Canada in favour of the sophisticated as opposed to the unsophisticated. We are biasing the tax system in favour of those who can afford to hire tax lawyers or tax accountants. The ordinary Canadian is even now more baffled by what the Government is attempting to do. Let me be clear, Mr. Speaker, because I think this is a very critical point. Bill C-80 makes the tax system of the country even more biased.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) made an interesting speech today when she introduced the Bill. She reminded me of Johnny Carson who tells a few jokes at the beginning of his show before he invites his guests to say something. I thought it was rather humorous when the Minister told the people of Canada that the reason we have to add more taxes on to construction materials, cable television, candies and pet foods, gasoline, beer, cigarettes, cigars and a variety of other goods is that we have to get the deficit down. Let us think about that for a moment, Mr. Speaker.
For the last number of weeks, we have been hearing time and time again of the need for bringing a Bill before Parliament that would provide for $875 million as the first instalment in the bail-out of the uninsured depositors of the failed Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. That is only the first instalment of the bail-out. In the end, it might amount to $1 billion, which is $1,000 million. It might amount to $2 billion in the end. We are not certain yet. We have to bail out depositors who should never be receiving the full amount of money. The Government is going to bail out
October 24, 1985

uninsured depositors, whether they be depositors in the Bank of Shanghai, the Bank of Hong Kong or the Bank of America. We will never know. These depositors are simply going to receive their cheques for $1 million, $2 million or $5 million from the taxpayers of Canada. That is a priority of the Government.
The Gulf deal is going to cost the taxpayers perhaps $1 billion for a major tax boondoggle. That is okay. Presumably it is acceptable. I can go on and on about the unbelievable tax boondoggles that apply to those folks who do not pay any income tax at all year after year. I am not talking about poor people, I am talking about people who have annual incomes in the range of $500,000 but are able to use the tax system to pay nothing year after year. You know, Mr. Speaker, because you are an intelligent man, that if these people do not pay any income tax or their fair share of income tax, who is paying more than their fair share? It is the ordinary Canadian citizen who cannot afford a tax lawyer or a tax accountant to do his or her tax planning.
Ordinary people make perhaps $25,000 per year and pay all of the taxes that are owing. There are no loopholes or tax expenditure exemptions for them. They pay through the nose year after year to make up for those folks who do not pay their fair share.

speechtext:
My friend, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), reminds me that on top of all of the giveaways and all of the billions of dollars the Government has shovelled out to people who are undeserving of it, we are asking people to pay an extra few cents for their gasoline.
The Minister has said that this measure is equitable because we are asking everyone to pay more sales tax. Poor people, rich people and middle-income people are all going to pay the same. It sounds equitable. However, a single parent with an annual income of $7,000 and an upper-income earner with an annual income of $400,000 will pay exactly the same tax when they go to the corner grocery store to buy some confectionery items. The poorest people of the country will be paying the same amount of tax as the richest people in the country when they purchase their goods. Is this equitable? Is this fair? Is this an honest approach to the tax system? Of course not.
There is something very insidious about Bill C-80. It results in a significant increase in the taxes on transportation fuel. In the coming year, these taxes will total $930 million. Again this tax on transportation fuel will apply to everyone. However, there are some regions of Canada in which the cost of transportation is of much more significance than it is in other regions. Canada is the second largest country in the world. In central Canada, the distances that are travelled are much shorter than those travelled in western Canada or particularly in northern Canada. This means that the tax on fuel is directly biased against western and northern Canada. In those areas, goods have to be transported over vast distances. We all know that when goods including refrigerators, mining equipment and oil rig equipment are transported over great distances,
Excise Tax Act
those costs are ultimately passed along to the consumer. This means that people in western and northern Canada will be paying more for their transportation costs and therefore by definition more for the items that are purchased and make up one's cost of living.
This is not a fair Bill. This is not a fair piece of taxation. It is quite the contrary. I do not know if the Minister really made her case when she defended the 7 per cent tax on construction material. Is this not the Party that said that it would be appropriate to take the taxes on construction materials away in order to provide an incentive for the construction industry and particularly the home construction industry of Canada?
When he was in opposition, I remember hearing my friend, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), rising on occasion after occasion to say that one of the answers to the economic problems of Canada was to encourage the home building sector because that would put a lot of people to work immediately, both directly and indirectly, through all the manufacturing sectors that provide for the housing industry. What does the Government do? It slaps a 7 per cent tax on construction materials. How is that going to assist the housing industry? How is it going to encourage more construction across the country? There may be some way that it will do so, and I would be interested to hear what Hon. Members from the Government side have to say about that.
When we add 7 per cent on to the cost of construction materials, 7 per cent on to the cost of cable and pay television services, 14 per cent on to the cost of alcoholic beverages, 14 per cent on to the cost of tobacco products and 11 per cent on to the cost of other taxable goods, the total package for the coming year will come to about $990 million. That is what it will cost Canadians in extra taxes.
Many people from Kamloops-Shuswap, the riding which I have the honour to represent, have asked me a question. 1 will raise this question here because I see that the Minister of State for Finance is present and is interested in the comments of Hon. Members. Perhaps I will pass along to her the questions that I have been receiving.
My constituents have told me that they are now struggling to get their businesses back on track, they are struggling to get their small farms or ranches going again or they are simply trying to get their lives together and are struggling to find part-time or temporary employment. They ask how it is that an increase in taxation will help this process. How is it that taking $990 million out of the pockets of Canadians will be of assistance in getting the economy of Kamloops-Shuswap going? It is not clear to me how that will work. As a matter of fact, I do not understand how taking money away from people will assist in generating wealth and economic activity in the regions of Canada.
When one looks at the Bill which is before us one sees two areas which are always hit, that is, tobacco and alcohol. It is a hard area to criticize as a politician. It is difficult for a politician to stand up and say: "We want to reduce the taxes

October 24, 1985
Excise Tax Act
on alcohol and cigarettes". Elowever, I would like to make a case for the tourist industry. If there is one industry in Canada which makes a great deal of sense when one looks at future possibilities in terms of economic development, it is the tourist industry of Canada. We have a magnificent country which people enjoy visiting. I do not think we have even begun to explore the potential for expanding this industry as a leading industry of the future. Currently, the industry employs about 600,000 Canadians, 60 per cent of whom are women employed in about 50,000 businesses. The industry involves a major factor in terms of foreign exchange for the country. Of course, the industry is suffering very seriously as a result of the recession. It suffers because the gas taxes keep rising and a great many of our American friends think twice about visiting the country because of the high costs of transportation, the high costs of accommodation and the high costs of beverages in our beverage rooms. I do not not want to make a big item out of this point; but when we talk to tourist operators we are told that the prices of drinks in lounges keep going up and up as a result of increased taxes. That is not a factor in terms of increasing the tourism industry. It is quite the contrary. It is a factor which makes the development of that industry very difficult indeed.
I wish to speak for a moment or two about the tax system itself. It is a system which is basically an honour system whereby people are expected to be honest and forthright. They fill out their tax returns to the best of their ability. Unfortunately, now that often requires help from outside advisers because those tax forms are so complex. I remember a previous Minister of Finance standing in his place one day and saying that even he could not fill out his tax return any longer because it was simply too complicated. Apparently, he was a simple man, at least that is what he said, and he needed outside help with his tax return. For the ordinary Canadian citizen it is a complex document, one which we all await to with horror now that we are approaching that time of year again. However, it is a system based on honour. It is based on the assumption that people will be honest and that they will clearly indicate their income and expenses, tally up their deductions and decide on the bottom line if they owe the Government more money, if they have paid adequately or if they can expect a return because of an overpayment.
This honour system is based on the assumption that the system is fair. In other words, you can only expect people to be honest if they sense that the system in which they are operating is an honest one that is not biased in favour of one group, region or industry as opposed to another. I want to say clearly that the people of Canada no longer believe that the tax system is fair. I have no hesitation in making that remark. I do not think anyone would dare stand up and say that the tax system of this country is fair. I have tried to make the point that increasing gasoline taxes is a bias against western and northern Canada where distance is such an important factor in the transportation of goods. In a sense it is a tax on distance. Those who happen to live far away from central Canada are being asked to pay more.
Then, we have a sales tax which is regressive. Regardless of whether someone is rich or poor he pays the same amount of money for a loaf of bread, a bottle of milk or whatever the case may be. Now when we buy Pamper cat food for our pets or seeds for our budgies we have to pay more taxes on that, for gosh sakes. I suggest that that is a very desperate bid indeed. The point is that the tax is regressive. It is punitive to the lower income people. Rich people do not mind paying a couple of cents more for a package of birdseed, for a bottle of milk or for a loaf of bread. However, for the poor people of the country it is a major factor.

speechtext:
My hon. friend from Vancouver reminds me of a devastating report which was released earlier this week indicating that, indeed, the rich in Canada are getting richer and that the poor are getting poorer and are becoming more numerous. I believe that there is now something in the neighbourhood of four million who are described by Statistics Canada as having an income which places them in the poverty category. That is a sad comment. It is also a sad comment when one considers that families earning more than $50,000 are actually creating 40 per cent of the wealth of the country. That is just a handful of people when one looks at the entire population. It just points to the fact that the rich are getting richer and the poor are getting poorer. Bill C-80 will simply add to that process because it is unfair legislation. It is an unfair tax levy.
The point I am trying to make is that our tax system is based on an honour system which assumes that the system is honest and fair to everyone. It assumes that it is equitable. It is not. What it means is that people no longer have faith in the Government. It means that they no longer have faith in the tax system. Therefore, the economy is moving underground. More and more transactions are being conducted with cash or through a barter system. For instance, a lawyer will say: "I will do some of your legal work and since you are a dentist you can do the dental work on my children's teeth". Or a plumber will say: "I will fix the plumbing in your rec room and you can come in and do a bit of masonry for me on my fireplace. We will not mention it and there will be no record of this transaction". As a result, no income tax or business tax is paid, as the case may be. How much of this is taking place in Canada today? Does anyone know of instances of this having taken place? Does anyone know of instances of abuse of the tax system? I suspect there is not a person who does not know of such an instance. This presents a serious challenge to the tax system of the country. It is a serious challenge to the country itself since $30 billion, $40 billion or $50 billion going underground annually also goes untaxed. With this unfair tax system it simply means that the Government has to go after those people who are paying the taxes. We know who they are. They are not the large corporations nor the upper income earners. They are Canada's ordinary tax-paying citizens. More and more the tax system has become biased against the average citizen of the country.
October 24, 1985

When I look through the Bill I notice that as a result of increased sales taxes effective next year the Government plans to raise $990 million out of the pockets of taxpayers. People will say that that money will be well spent because services will be received for it. The point is that there will not be any additional services because the Government is cutting back on traditional services which the people of the country have come to expect.
The Government even tried to cut back on increases to old age pensions. I remember the day the Government came in and said it was about to bail out two banks and that it was giving tax boondoggles to the big oil companies as part of the Western Accord. I believe that will amount to something in the order of $9 billion over the next five years. The Government gives away these vast amounts of money, billions and billions of dollars, and in doing so it has to collect more taxes. Thus, the Government said that it would hold back on increasing senior citizens' pensions. It took the same stand with respect to increasing family allowances. As a result of a massive public outcry, thank goodness, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) realized he had made a disastrous decision and he forgot about capping the increases on old age pensions to allow pensioners to at least keep up with the cost of living. However, that is not the case with family allowances. The children of Canada will have to pay, if you like, for the giveaways which this Government has made to large oil companies, foreign banks and the like.
Only a 1 per cent increase in the sales tax involves $990 million coming out of the pockets of Canadians. Broadening of the federal sales tax will take another half a billion dollars out of the taxpayers' pockets. Actual tax increases will result in $990 million being paid out of the taxpayers' pockets-basically out of the consumers' pockets, which means that the people living in Kamloops will not have that money to buy some goods or purchase some service. That money will not be circulating time and time again in that community; it will be pulled out down here to Ottawa. I do not see how that move will help small communities across the country, the rural areas or even the large cities. The alcohol and tobacco excise taxes in this coming year will result in $240 million being raised in additional taxes from this sector.
What does it all mean? When one takes into account the sales tax it means that an average household with an income of $15,000 will be paying out $140 more in sales tax. If one's income is in the $20,000 range, it means paying out an extra $282 in taxes. A household which earns $40,000 a year pays about $361 in increased tax burden in the upcoming year. This means that these dollars will not be in circulation in the small communities and regions throughout the country. They will be focused in Ottawa to assist in attempts at deficit reduction, particularly now with the deficit increasing as a result of these massive giveaways.
There is another interesting point with respect to our tax system. There is no question that people do not pay the same
Excise Tax Act
tax. Mr. MacEachen, the former Liberal Minister of Finance, brought in a Budget which resulted in a reduction in the rate of tax paid by the upper income earners. He thought that those people in the $200,000 or $300,000 a year income level were paying too much tax, so he dropped the rates down. That lost us hundreds of millions of dollars in uncollected taxes. That is what he left us with.
The new Minister of Finance thought that some people who make money through capital gains should not even be taxed at all. Let the person who is a miner, a logger, a fisherman, an office worker or a teacher be taxed on whatever amount of money he or she makes. If they make $30,000 or $35,000, they should pay a proportionate share of tax, with a minimum amount of loopholes if any. But those people who make money through capital gains should be exempt to a point. That flies directly in the face of the report of the Carter Commission. It looked into the tax system, and at the top of the list of things it said we must do in this country is to recognize that a buck is a buck, that a dollar of income is a dollar of income regardless of how it is earned and that it should be taxed as a dollar. At the top of the list of the Carter Commission was the recommendation that capital gains should be taxed as any other income. When there is no income tax at all up to $500,000 in lifetime capital gains-and we are talking about a very select group of Canadians-then ordinary working Canadians will have to pay, therefore, more tax than they should because someone has to make up the difference.
The Minister of Finance made a speech to the Canadian Tax Foundation on November 28, 1984, wherein he stated, and I quote:
Our recent figures indicate that the effect of tax incentives has been to reduce the average federal corporate income tax rate from 36 per cent to 15 per cent. . . Particular activities qualify for very high rates of incentives, especially under certain grant programs. When the benefits from special tax incentives are added we are looking, in some cases, at an extraordinary generous level of assistance.
That is nice for the corporate sector. It has had its effective tax rate drop from 36 per cent down to 15 per cent. Was that not a nice gesture, Mr. Speaker? Again, there is a certain group in the business community which is considered as being entitled to a significant drop in the effective tax rate. To the struggling logger or truck driver out there in the regions, this would be interesting news.
The accelerated capital cost allowance allows a business to write off against income depreciation of assets at a faster rate than is actually the case. This cost us back in 1981 about $2 billion. What this does is to give an incentive to a corporation to use capital instead of labour. The Government is saying that because you can write down the cost of your equipment, rather than hire people, you should purchase and install equipment. This incentive should certainly be questioned at the time of the high unemployment we are facing today.
The boondoggle which the previous Government brought in was the scientific research tax credit. That cost us in 1984 about $2 billion, through quick flipping, whereby corporations could sell their research tax credits even though the research was never done. One could go on and on, Mr. Speaker, but it gets depressing after a while. Once we start looking at this tax

October 24, 1985
Excise Tax Act
Act, all we keep finding are pages and pages of tax exemptions for certain kinds of people and for certain kinds of economic activities.
There is one group of people who is almost always excluded from any kind of tax incentive or loophole, and that is the ordinary Canadian. They are not taken into consideration in the tax Act or in legislation such as Bill C-80 when tax changes are made. We cannot say that loud enough, Mr. Speaker, and we have to say it time and time again until the Government starts to accept responsibility and does something in terms of developing a more equitable tax system.
The Minister of Finance had this to say about the tax system, and I quote:
As we grapple with the technicalities, the subtleties and the complexities of our tax system, we must never lose sight of the citizens it is ultimately meant to serve. That is what our efforts are all about. The real bottom line is people.
What he did not say is which people he is talking about. What he meant was that certain kinds of people were the beneficiaries of all of these subtleties and complexities of our tax system-not the ordinary Canadian, but a very privileged few in our society and within our business community. It is not the struggling small business person who is being rewarded or encouraged or who is receiving incentives through the tax system. The most tragic example of that was a few years ago when both Shell and the Bank of Montreal used the tax system to pay no income tax at all in spite of significantly large profits.
This is the kind of system which we must recognize is in existence and when the Government stands up and tells it is introducing Bill C-80 today in an effort to bring equity and fairness to the tax system, we must recognize that that is absolute balderdash. We cannot have equity and fairness built into a system when we increase the sales tax which, by definition, is regressive and punishes those people who are least able to afford paying taxes at all.
I would be remiss today if I did not raise one important point about tax discounters. It is the time of the year when we start filling out tax forms. A rather insidious practice has developed over the last number of years and it is growing very rapidly as people realize that the tax system is so complex that they cannot fill out their tax form and must have some help. More importantly, the tax discounters thrive on the victims of oppressive economic times, who include the poorest people in society who are eligible for such items as the refundable child tax credit. A single parent, for example, knows that because of the family's low income and the child tax credit, there will be a refund after the income tax form is filed. Single parents are desperately in need of cash because they are inevitably living below the poverty line. They go to the tax discounters who tell them they will give them cash for the privilege of filling out their tax return and sending it away. In other words, the tax discounters make their money helping those people fill out their tax forms, giving them a portion of what they are entitled to and keeping the rest as a fee for their service. That is a terrible situation, Mr. Speaker.
It is hard to believe that a Government which is seriously interested in equity and fairness would permit such a thing to take place. There are many countries which abandoned this type of practice because they realized it preyed upon those least able to afford paying out a portion of their tax refund. Many Hon. Members have pleaded for an end to this practice, especially the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North, who has repeatedly in the House asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) when he is going to move to bring in a Bill to prohibit this exploitive practice, and after hearing time and time again from the Liberal administration that it would be getting around to that sometime, he hears the same thing from this Government. In the meantime this practice grows and victimizes more and more people who can ill afford to pay that kind of price to these tax discounters.
In conclusion, Bill C-80 comes at a very inappropriate time. Canadians are struggling to get on their feet and are doing what they can to encourage economic activity in their own communities. They are working very, very hard and, I might say, going to some extraordinary lengths to ensure that economic prosperity returns for them and their families. It is a very delicate and difficult struggle, yet the Government introduces a Bill which will result in hundreds upon hundreds of millions of dollars being taken from the pockets of those same people. There are increases in sales taxes, gasoline taxes, and confectionery goods taxes. It is a very inappropriate step for the Government to be taking. It is difficult to encourage people to remain optimistic and hopeful when, on the one hand, the Government says we must all sacrifice and then, on the other hand, it brings in a Bill which asks ordinary people to sacrifice even more than they already have.
As for myself and my colleagues in the NDP, we certainly do not support the Bill and we will vote against it. Quite frankly, we have many, many questions about its details. Since this, unfortunately, is an opportunity to talk only about the Bill in principle, we will be looking forward to examining the logic of those clauses which exempt certain kinds of goods from federal sales tax but not others. We will have an opportunity in committee to look at those details, but at this point in time we certainly do not support this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am both pleased and saddened to participate in this debate on Bill C-80. Saddened, because unfortunately we now have to face the music-the S200 billion deficit which our Liberal predecessors left the country saddled with as a result of their indecent mismanagement. Yet they are the ones who now want us to account for the measures we want to take in an attempt to get Canada back on the right track. Pleased, because I want to support the approach taken in this case by our Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall).
What did we say on September 4, 1984? That we would promote national reconciliation, economic renewal and
October 24, 1985

renewed Canadian internationalism. Mr. Speaker, we must not lose sight of the general rules. Practically every time we advocate new propositions, the Liberals especially have so little foresight that they get lost in details without ever dealing with guiding principles or traditional economic precepts. I happen to know they have competent spokesmen in that field, but for some unknown reason they seem to lose their bearings when they become politicians. We had promised to restore a climate of national reconciliation, and the starting point was the Western Accord which led to a significant economic upsurge in that part of the country. I see the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow) is in the House, and I am sure she would attest to the economic revival of her region since the Western Accord, in contrast with the days when the Liberals never missed a chance to create a wide gap between the interests of the central Government and those of Western Canada.
And then the agreement with Newfoundland was a historic occasion. The Liberals had been dragging their feet for years and years, but we did settle the issue as we had promised during the election campaign before September 4.
Since we came to office a good many Quebecers have seen the futility of the separatist option and took stock of their Canadian heritage. In that respect we have to wonder today whether the proponents of separatism did not stand to further their cause by playing the game of the Liberal Government. The dust settled after our election and separatism is on the wane.
We had also promised economic renewal. We are now beginning to feel the impact of our politicies in this regard. We have seen 340,000 new jobs being created in the last year. Unemployment and interest rates have gone down. Inflation is under control. Inflation rates of 10, 12 or 13 per cent had serious repercussions on the most disadvantaged in our society and on senior citizens in families with very low incomes. At the time, the Liberals did not want to index the social benefits enjoyed by Canadians. However, we are now beating inflation, with rates of around 4 or 4.5 per cent, which means that the most needy among us can have a nearly constant standard of living. There is also a positive picture in the increase of the gross national product which continues to surprise the experts and to surpass the forecasts of economists.
On September 4, 1984, the Canadian public gave us a very formal official and significant mandate asking us to tighten our belts and reduce our budgetary deficit. There are now 211 representatives of Canadian men and women in this House to fulfil this mandate. At the time, we told the Canadian population that it would not be easy because we had inherited a difficult situation and the building was on fire. This fire had been burning since the Liberals had been in power. They left us a deficit of $200 billion. They had forgotten that the role of a Government is to distribute part of the public resources to the most needy. They modernized somewhat too quickly. They
Excise Tax Act
decided to distribute public borrowings, not only to the needy, but also to companies, wealthy people and their friends. We saw crown corporations vote themselves extraordinary amounts for their administrators. There was the unfortunate example of the Canada Post Corporation. This corporation, under Liberal administration, has 17 vice-presidents who each have their own car and chauffeur. It is quite a sight to go to the headquarters of the Canada Post Corporation and to see all those cars with chauffeurs. You would think it is a much more important corporation. This shows the mismanagement of the Liberals and how they were able to accumulate a deficit of $200 billion.
They made excessive investments, created a paper empire and left us with only constraints. The Liberals are gone, but we are faced with expenditures of $105 billion. How is this money spent? We spend $25 billion, or 25c. on each dollar, to pay the interests on the borrowings of the Liberals, some of which were distributed among wealthy Canadians and their own friends.
We also spend $45 billion, or another 45c. out of each dollar if we are speaking about a budget of $105 billion, for social welfare programs. The Liberals are now asking us not to increase the revenues of our Government. These $45 billion allocated to social programs represent 57 per cent of the expenditures of the Canadian Government if we exclude interest charges on the debt. Therefore, 57c. on each dollar, or more than half of our revenues, are spent to help the most needy Canadians, out of a total budget of $105 billion. There therefore remains $35 billion which must be distributed among all the other departments and Government programs.
We inherited a technically disastrous situation as concerns Canadian Armed Forces which need to be modernized. However, we must operate within very restrictive budgetary limits.
What have been the effects of this mismanagement by our predecessors? All Canadian men and women lost whatever incentive they might have had. They could gain nothing by being creative as they were being stifled by Government regulations and constraints. Our entrepreneurs, and about 15 per cent of the labour force in a country should be in this category, lost all incentive during the last decades. They have practically disappeared from this country.
Because of the runaway inflation that prevailed under the Liberal administration, our productivity has decreased, and we can no longer sell our products abroad-except for our natural resources because they were always willing to sell our natural resources abroad-we shut ourselves out from external markets.
What are the solutions to the problems we inherited from Liberals? The first one is for Canadian men and women to tighten their belts, an effort that must be made by each and every one of us in Canada.

October 24, 1985
Excise Tax Act
We have seen a significant example of this belt-tightening exercise when the Prime Minister decided to have his salary reduced by 15 per cent when he came to power. When all Cabinet Ministers in this Government accepted to have their own salaries reduced by 10 per cent as an effort at national restraint. It can be emphasized, Mr. Speaker, that no such effort was ever made or agreed upon by the Opposition Leader or the Leader of the New Democratic Party. They are asking us to make all those efforts, they get them from the people, but they themselves fail to set the example.
To this day, our solutions have brought about results. We have our 340,000 new jobs. Entrepreneur confidence has returned. We are now in the process, through collective efforts, of reviving an economy that was in a most unhealthy state, a state which the Liberals have brought about and which they would have gladly kept going for a few more years to come.
But under the laws of economics it was impossible to go any further, this country could no longer borrow money. Our people, in such a declining state of affairs, could sustain no additional effort. It was therefore essential to create a new climate, and this is what we did. Our goal is to have balanced budgets from year to year, positive cash flows as between revenues and expenditures. This is one of the only means of putting the economy back on its feet. It is imperative that this country regain confidence, that our citizens wake up, and this is the climate we are providing.
Mr. Speaker, reference had also been made to our international openness, from coast to coast, a new economic impetus, an international outlook.
As recently as the day before yesterday, our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), to all intents and purposes, won the day at the meeting of member states of the British Commonwealth. Our Prime Minister asserted himself following his first year of public life and assumed the leadership within the Commonwealth, suggesting at that recent meeting concrete steps for helping to settle the crisis experienced in South Africa.
When reference is made to the international involvement of our country, it should also be pointed out that in New York our Prime Minister yesterday delivered before the world powers one of most straightforward and significant message on disarmement.
Our Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) is now trying hard to give Canadian within the next 20 years the best record as far as developing our international trade is concerned, opening up the largest and most powerful market in the world, the American market.
Mr. Speaker, for all those reasons, we must amend our legislation to continue to give Canadian men and women a clear indication that we want to carry out our programs and this legislation is merely aimed at giving them what they asked for on September 4. We are giving them a chance to tighten their belt so that after that short term effort, we will benefit
from it thanks to a new economic impetus, the welfare of Canadians and the international prestige of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-80 now under consideration is completely useless in my opinion and could have been avoided if this Government had taken a different approach. We are told that this Bill was introduced, as the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) has just said, because the Canadian public gave his Government, or at least his party, the mandate to make all Canadians tighten their belts. I think that all Canadian men and women were aware of the fact that, after the worst economic crisis ever in Canada and the other industrialized countries in 1981 and 1982, we would have a serious public debt problem.
My first criticism of this Government would be that it did not take this fact into account during the 1984 electoral campaign. Who made promises representing additional expenditures of $20 billion according to the figures of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie)? Those promises were not made by the Liberals, but by the Conservatives themselves. Who promised during the electoral campaing, for instance, to solve the oil problem and especially to do something for the private retailers who do not work for the big oil companies? It was not the party on this side, but the party opposite. Yet, after criticizing the Petro-Canada problem for so many years, what did they do after coming to power? They invested even more money, allowed Petro-Canada to spend even more, and because of this, a refinery in eastern Montreal will close its doors, 450 jobs will disappear, and in addition, all private gasoline retailers in Quebec will be facing even larger cartels than before.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that this Bill could been avoided if the Government had taken a different course of action. I am aware that the public debt is serious. I am aware that 25 per cent of our expenditures, or 25 cents out of each dollar, are used to pay interest charges on the debt. However, if this is so, why not have worked on this angle?
Why is it, for instance, that the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine), the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tell us that we must reduce the deficit? What did they do in the budget? Why do we now have to examine such a piece of legislation? Why will all Canadians have to pay taxes on nonproprietary medicine? Why will Canadians have to pay higher taxes on gasoline? Why will they have to pay taxes on building materials, such as pre-mixed concrete? Why do we have to do this? It is very simple. It is because this Government decided to give money to the multinationals and make the taxpayers pay for it.
It must be emphasized that this is the basic philosophical difference between the Conservatives and my own party.
According to the Conservative philosophy, one should give to the rich and tax medium- and lower-income groups, and keep hoping that within the next 10 or 15 years the rich will be
rich enough to spend, and that ultimately they will create jobs for the poor. That, of course, is the story of the horse and the sparrow, as has often been explained. We on this side think that the best way to ensure a distribution of wealth, a more democratic, more liberal way, is to make sure that wealth is distributed more adequately and that the rich pay more, so that we may maintain a better and fairer balance in wealth distribution among all middle-income groups, especially in the less favoured regions, and this involves regional development.
They say they want to tackle the deficit, but what are they doing in the Budget? They did away with the tax on oil multinationals, and this means that by 1990, $8.5 billion will have slipped out of this Government's coffers into those of ten odd oil multinational corporations. I repeat it: $8.5 billion. They decided to do away with the tax on capital gains, and certainly people earning $25,000 and $30,000 a year do not earn enough capital gains to benefit from that deduction offered by the Conservatives. You know something, Mr. Speaker? By 1990, it is nearly $5 billion that will have gone out of the Canadian Government's coffers into those of a mere 4 per cent of Canadian taxpayers who had capital gains over these last years and will now get those tax benefits.
What have we done to that Government? We are told: Middle-income Canadians, tighten your belts! And at the same time, they decide all of a sudden to take close to $ 1 billion out of the pockets of Canadian taxpayers so that the Government may reimburse nameless depositors, individuals or companies, or foreign banks that had deposited more than $60,000 in the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are asked to tighten their belts. Middle-income and lower-income Canadians are asked to pay a higher sales tax. The Government has enough money to forego potential tax revenues of something like $1 billion- some say it is even more-for the benefit of a couple of shareholders in a company that just bought the Canadian assets of Gulf, which may amount to $1 billion in tax expenditures, and then they say it was just an administrative decision. We read in the papers that the former Deputy Minister of Finance clearly stated that his Minister allowed him to keep from discussing the issue because of the possibility he might work with the Reichmanns, and his Minister was kind enough to look after that matter himself. And we are being asked to believe, today, after the tainted tuna affair and the banks affair that those people speak the truth and only the truth and that neither the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), nor the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), nor the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mrs. Carney) knew about that administrative decision which handed out $1 billion to a few shareholders of a big company. And also we are asked to pass legislation which will force Canadians to tighten their belts.
Mr. Speaker, nothing much has been said in the House about another issue which was discussed at the same time as Domtar, in the Eastern Townships, an issue which had my colleagues for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) and the member for Granby-Stanstead-Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) working very hard. The Government did not want to give a cent. Finally,

And today, the Hon. And they want us to believe that today, Mr. Speaker.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that there is a limit to trying to stuff people like suitcases. I think that truth must be clearly stated. If we look at the impact the Bill will have by 1990, it all means that this Government is going to take $16 billion more out of the pockets of Canadian taxpayers, and I would rather not go on again about the sales tax, which we all know is going to hurt low income families far more, proportionally, than other Canadians. All this is going to add up to $16 billion. And you know what? The special benefits for oil multinationals, which add up to $8.5 billion, capital gains-$5 billion, the Algoma deal-$200 million, plus one billion dollars' worth of "advance ruling" for Reichmann and one billion dollars in the bank fiasco, do you realize that all this adds up to $16 billion? And the sum total of this whole exercise is, that this Government's deficit will not be reduced by a single cent. In fact, it will increase.
To the Hon. Member for Levis who says that the Government is doing this to bring down the deficit, I say this: It's like trying to water your garden when you turn on the water but you don't open the nozzle. It won't do much for your garden and it won't do much for the deficit. And the worst part is that all these cash payments and foregone revenues benefit exclusively a certain privileged class, and I am referring to the oil multinationals, the big banks and people with deposits of $60,000 and up. The benefits go to the people who buy a company and manage a tax benefit of one billion dollars.
Mr. Speaker, all this money goes into the hands of... I think if I had two more hands, if I could find two extra hands, I could almost show what these people are like.
Unfortunately, 10 or 11 million Canadian taxpayers are probably going to have to pay the bill. And that is the whole philosophy of this Government. They think they can activate the economy by taking money from those who have less-and I am referring to the middle class and those with very low incomes-to give it to the rich.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that this economic assumption is wrong, that it will create social problems in Quebec and in Canada, and that it will also create problems for regional development in this country, because in a country like Canada, we cannot expect the market to meet all the needs of our various regions.
